chapters.title: Chapter 5: The Oldest Dream

passages.chapter-05-p-fb311e2a3a: The story begins three centuries before anyone imagined a computer.
passages.chapter-05-p-2db12eb263: In 1679, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz — the co-inventor of calculus, diplomat, philosopher, polymath — sketched out a vision that wouldn't be realized for three hundred years. He called it the characteristica universalis: a universal symbolic language that could represent all human knowledge, paired with a calculus ratiocinator: a mechanical procedure for reasoning about that knowledge.
passages.chapter-05-p-06ba151512: Assign unique symbols to every concept. Define rules for combining them. Then, when philosophers disagree, they needn't argue — they could simply say, "Calculemus!" Let us calculate! The truth would emerge from the manipulation of symbols, as certain as arithmetic.
passages.chapter-05-p-ae7da67464: Leibniz even imagined a machine for this purpose. He'd already built a mechanical calculator — more sophisticated than Pascal's, capable of multiplication and division. Why not a machine for thought itself? "The human race will have a new kind of instrument," he wrote, "which will increase the power of the mind much more than optical lenses strengthen the eyes."
passages.chapter-05-p-3745d36b42: He never built it. He couldn't have — the engineering didn't exist. But Leibniz articulated binary arithmetic, logical operations, and the conviction that thought itself could be reduced to calculation. Every computer in the world runs on the architecture he imagined in a century that still lit its streets with candles.
passages.chapter-05-p-e175984a3c: He died in 1716, largely forgotten. His funeral was attended by his secretary and no one else. The dream would sleep for 138 years.

chapters.title: Chapter 6: The Brachistochrone

passages.chapter-09-p-cb692b7544: On the afternoon of 26 January 1697, Isaac Newton came home from the Royal Mint. He had been Warden of the Mint for nine months — appointed by the Treasury to oversee the Great Recoinage, a logistical operation that had him supervising the destruction of nearly the entire English currency and its replacement with new milled coins. He left the Tower of London around four. Waiting for him was a parcel from Switzerland.
passages.chapter-09-p-a7d94fdfd6: Inside was a printed challenge, six months old, addressed to "the keenest mathematicians flourishing throughout the world." The author was Johann Bernoulli of Basel. The problem, stated in plain Latin, was this: given two points A and B in a vertical plane, with B lower than A but not directly below it, find the curve along which a heavy bead, sliding under gravity from A, will reach B in the shortest possible time. Bernoulli called the unknown curve the brachistochrone — from the Greek for shortest time. He had set the deadline at six months. Five had already passed. Newton's copy had taken its time crossing the Channel.
passages.chapter-09-p-adfefd35eb: He started after dinner. He finished at four in the morning. The next day he sent the solution to the Royal Society anonymously.
passages.chapter-09-p-54789e73c6: When the Philosophical Transactions printed the unsigned solution in February, Bernoulli read it and said one sentence in Latin: tanquam ex ungue leonem. "I recognize the lion by his claw." He knew who had answered him.
passages.chapter-09-p-855b3f1606: The story is too clean to be entirely true — the official Newton biographies note that he had been thinking about the problem on and off for months, and the "single night" is a polished version put about by his niece. A 55-year-old man, half a continent away, glanced at a problem that the foremost mathematicians of Europe had spent half a year on, and solved it before going to bed.
passages.chapter-09-p-06ea14c16a: Newton was not the only solver. Bernoulli himself published his own solution. So did his brother Jakob, with whom he was carrying on a long and bitter mathematical feud. So did Leibniz, with whom Newton was carrying on his own. So did the Marquis de l'Hôpital, who had paid Bernoulli for the calculus lessons he was now publishing as his own. Five solutions, by five different methods, arriving at the same curve. The curve was a cycloid — the shape traced by a fixed point on the rim of a wheel rolling along a straight line. Roll a wheel; mark the point. The path it sweeps in the air is, of all possible paths between its endpoints, the one a bead will slide along fastest under gravity.
passages.chapter-09-p-b32c6f8bbd: This was an unexpected result. The straight line is the shortest distance between two points; the cycloid is not the shortest. But the bead is faster on the cycloid because the early steep drop converts gravitational potential into speed quickly, and the rest of the curve cashes that speed in.
passages.chapter-09-p-6def7ed221: What mattered was not the answer but that an answer existed. The question — of all the curves between A and B, which minimizes time? — turned out to have a precise mathematical answer derivable by general methods. The methods opened a field. Calculus of variations was born in the months around the brachistochrone challenge, and over the next half-century Leonhard Euler made it systematic.
passages.chapter-09-p-2fda56c542: Euler's 1744 book had a long Latin title that translates to A Method for Finding Curves Enjoying the Property of Maximum or Minimum. It set out what would later be called the Euler–Lagrange equation, the engine that converts any minimization problem on functions into a differential equation you can sometimes solve. Euler thought the engine described the deep structure of the world. His preface contains the line that the book has been moving toward for a century: "Since the fabric of the universe is most perfect, and is the work of a most wise Creator, nothing whatsoever takes place in the universe in which some rule of maximum or minimum does not appear." Two pages later he is computing the shape of a hanging chain.
passages.chapter-09-p-17ad7f5e1b: The same year, Pierre-Louis Maupertuis, in Paris, generalized the claim. He proposed that all of physics rests on a single principle: nature acts so as to minimize a quantity he called action, the integral of energy over time. Light refracts so that the time taken from source to eye is least, as Fermat had shown a century before. A planet's orbit minimizes action across the path. A chain hangs so as to minimize potential energy. Maupertuis offered the principle as direct proof of God's wisdom — God arranges nature to be economical. Voltaire mocked him in a pamphlet, Diatribe du docteur Akakia, that ended Maupertuis's reputation in salons and never quite let him recover.
passages.chapter-09-p-ccf8ea7c70: The mockery did not touch the mathematics. In 1755 a nineteen-year-old in Turin named Joseph-Louis Lagrange wrote to Euler with an algebraic reformulation that did away with the geometric reasoning the older man had used. Euler, who could have published the same result first, instead wrote back, withheld his own work, and let Lagrange publish. Thirty-three years later Lagrange completed Mécanique analytique, a book that contained, by his own boast, not a single diagram — the whole of mechanics rewritten as the search for stationary points of an integral. Hamilton extended the framework in 1834. Twentieth-century quantum mechanics would inherit the same machinery; the modern derivation of every physical theory begins by writing down an action and finding what minimizes it.
passages.chapter-09-p-de23e8b9a5: A different optimization tradition was running alongside, on simpler problems. In 1736 Euler, again, had solved the puzzle of whether one could walk through the city of Königsberg crossing each of its seven bridges exactly once. He showed it was impossible by abstracting the geography into a graph — points connected by lines — and asking about the parity of the connections. He had invented graph theory. The first explicit shortest-path question on a graph would be posed by another Bernoulli — Daniel, Johann's son — in studies of routing. The full algorithm would have to wait for Edsger Dijkstra in 1956, when computers made the question urgent. But the conceptual move was already in place by the mid-eighteenth century: many real problems, from circuit design to logistics, reduce to finding the shortest path through a network of choices.
passages.chapter-09-p-e95511b153: By the time Gauss came to the asteroid Ceres in 1801, he was working inside a tradition a century and a half old. Nature optimizes, the eighteenth century had decided. Light minimizes time, mass minimizes action, falling bodies trace the curve of least time, hanging chains find the shape of least potential energy. The mathematicians had given the practice of optimization a body of methods: write down what you want minimized, take the derivative, set it equal to zero, solve. When Gauss minimized the sum of squared errors on the asteroid observations, he was using a method whose intellectual lineage ran back through Lagrange, Euler, and the unsigned cycloid in the Philosophical Transactions of February 1697. When Cauchy in 1847 proposed following the gradient downhill on intractable problems, he was extending the same tradition to cases where the closed-form derivation could not be done.
passages.chapter-09-p-28f9f3283a: The brachistochrone was not a special problem. It was the founding statement of a general program: that the world has shapes, and the shapes are extremal. Three centuries later, every neural network on earth runs gradient descent on a loss function — and is, in the most direct possible sense, the brachistochrone problem with billions of variables, solved not by Newton overnight but by GPUs over weeks.

chapters.title: Chapter 7: Hume

passages.chapter-08-p-571a8aaf2a: In 1734, a 23-year-old Scotsman named David Hume left Edinburgh for the French town of La Flèche, in Anjou, where Descartes had gone to school a century before. He had suffered what we would call a nervous breakdown the previous year, brought on by reading too much philosophy too quickly; he had spent months unable to think clearly, and his doctors had prescribed exercise, claret, and a change of scene. He took the prescription, then ignored it, and spent the next three years in a Jesuit library writing a book.
passages.chapter-08-p-88e249e2d0: The book he came out of La Flèche with, in 1737, was A Treatise of Human Nature. He was twenty-six. It was the most ambitious philosophical project written in English in a hundred years. He sold it to a London publisher and waited.
passages.chapter-08-p-7990313e3d: Nothing happened. The Treatise appeared in 1739 and 1740, in three volumes, and was, in Hume's own phrase forty years later, "dead-born from the press" — it sold poorly, was barely reviewed, and the few reviews it did get missed the point. Hume was thirty when he understood that the work he had wagered his early adulthood on had failed. He went home to his family's Berwickshire estate, took a tutoring job, and started rewriting his arguments in shorter, more digestible English. The mature versions — An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding in 1748 and An Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals in 1751 — made him famous. The book that contained the original arguments stayed mostly unread until the nineteenth century.
passages.chapter-08-p-075fe7819a: The original arguments are what this book has been quietly building on.
passages.chapter-08-p-df840b6bf4: Hume examined how our ideas and expectations arise from experience. We say fire causes smoke, or that one billiard ball causes another to move. What do we actually observe? Events following events, repeatedly. We do not observe a necessary connection as an additional object beside them. Repetition produces an expectation in us. Hume presses the question of where our confidence in necessity comes from; the further implications of his account for causation in the world remain disputed among his readers.
passages.chapter-08-p-a5cc863751: Predictive models make the force of the question tangible. Predicting an event correctly does not, by itself, reveal why it happened. A model learning that umbrellas accompany rain differs from an account of what would happen if we distributed umbrellas on a sunny day. To distinguish them, we need information about mechanisms, interventions, or additional assumptions. Machine learning is not confined to association, but any method going beyond it owes us an account of where the extra step comes from. This is the induction question introduced in Chapter 4, now close enough to touch in a working system.
passages.chapter-08-p-fb4a781b35: Hume's next move was harder. If experience is all we have, what about the self that has the experiences? Hume looked. He said: when I introspect, I never catch myself directly. I catch a thought, a feeling, a perception. The self I thought I was looking for turns out to be a collection — a bundle — of these perceptions, with no glue except their succession in time. There is no unitary observer; there is the stream and the conviction that there is an observer of the stream, but the conviction is one more item in the stream. The self is a fiction the perceptions tell.
passages.chapter-08-p-58e493aaaf: When an LLM says “I,” the old question returns in a new voice. But a stream of tokens is not Hume’s stream of perceptions: whether the machine has experience is precisely what remains at issue. The resemblance gives us a reason to examine its first-person language. It supplies neither a certificate of a self nor a proof that a self is impossible.
passages.chapter-08-p-2dcd26ca74: The third move is the one the book's Part IV will lean on directly. In the second book of the Treatise, Hume wrote: "Reason is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions, and can never pretend to any other office than to serve and obey them." The line has been misread for two and a half centuries as a celebration of unreason. It is not. Hume is making a structural claim about where ends come from. Reason can tell you how to get what you want. It cannot tell you what to want. Wants come from somewhere outside reason — from biology, from habit, from upbringing, from the constitution of the kind of creature you are. A system with no wants would have nothing for reason to be in the service of. The alignment problem the book reaches in Chapter 48 is Hume's claim rewritten in engineering: optimization can be perfect, and the optimized output still wrong, because the loss function comes from somewhere reason cannot generate.
passages.chapter-08-p-cc1d139f9d: Hume died on 25 August 1776, in Edinburgh, of intestinal cancer. James Boswell, who liked deathbed conversions, went to see him a few weeks before, hoping to find a famous atheist terrified. He found Hume cheerful, joking about the boatman Charon refusing to take him because he had unfinished philosophical work. Adam Smith, who had been his closest friend for thirty years, wrote a letter to their common publisher describing the death — Hume's serenity, his curiosity about whether his books would still be selling in a century, his calm refusal to make peace with a God he did not believe in. Smith said later that the letter cost him more outrage than the entire Wealth of Nations. He had described a man dying well without religion, and a great many readers were not prepared to accept that as something a man could do.
passages.chapter-08-p-dcda092fef: The Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion appeared in 1779, three years after Hume’s death. They examined arguments from design for God’s existence. Darwin read the Dialogues in 1838, after returning from the Beagle voyage in 1836. Questions about design would meet his long work on explaining the diversity of living things.
passages.chapter-08-p-1eb58916d7: Hume leaves us in an uncomfortable position: we must act, while the evidence supplies no deductive certainty about what comes next. An astronomer who has lost an asteroid cannot wait for the philosophical problem to be solved. He has to point the telescope somewhere.

chapters.title: Chapter 8: Gauss and Cauchy

passages.chapter-10-p-49b089a937: On January 1, 1801, the Sicilian astronomer Giuseppe Piazzi pointed his telescope at a faint moving object in the constellation Taurus and recorded it as a new star. Over the next forty-one nights he watched it shift against the background of fixed stars until illness, and then the glare of the sun, took it away from him. He had observed it for nine degrees of arc. By the time European astronomers learned what he had found, the object — Ceres, the first known asteroid — was lost in the daylight sky.
passages.chapter-10-p-8c54f6e3ba: Predicting where a body will reappear from forty-one days of observation is not a problem classical celestial mechanics was equipped to solve. The standard methods needed long arcs and good initial conditions. Piazzi had given the world neither. Across the autumn of 1801, astronomers in Paris, Milan, and Bremen produced predictions that disagreed with each other by tens of degrees — wide enough that the search would be hopeless.
passages.chapter-10-p-ab4ea35039: A twenty-four-year-old mathematician in Brunswick named Carl Friedrich Gauss took the same forty-one observations and computed an orbit. His prediction placed Ceres in a small patch of sky near the constellation Virgo on the night of December 31, 1801. Franz Xaver von Zach, observing from Gotha, pointed his telescope at the patch Gauss had named and found the asteroid within half a degree of the predicted position. The method Gauss had used he would not publish for another eight years, in his 1809 Theoria motus corporum coelestium. He called it the method of least squares: given a set of observations that disagree, find the curve whose summed squared error against the data is smallest. The orbit that least disagrees with the observations is the best one you can have.
passages.chapter-10-p-8899c7d0dd: Gauss was a strange man to do this. He kept his notebooks closed. He had derived non-Euclidean geometry decades before Lobachevsky and Bolyai published it and never printed his own work, because he could not get the foundations to a state he found unembarrassing. Pauca sed matura was the motto on his seal — few, but ripe. He refused to publish until the mathematics was, in his own judgment, finished. Frege, working seventy years later in Jena, would inherit something of the same temperament and try to apply it to logic itself — to a domain where every consequence had to be deduced from foundations beyond doubt. The least-squares method is the opposite move. It does not ask what is true; it asks what is the smallest disagreement you can get away with.
passages.chapter-10-p-d0429a8d5c: Forty-six years later, in 1847, the French mathematician Augustin-Louis Cauchy published a four-page note in the Comptes rendus of the Paris Academy with the unremarkable title Méthode générale pour la résolution des systèmes d'équations simultanées. Cauchy was already famous; he had given analysis its modern epsilon-delta foundations, written six hundred papers, and held a chair at the Collège de France. The 1847 note is one of the least cited of his major works. What it describes is gradient descent.
passages.chapter-10-p-7022fc7fbb: The problem Cauchy was solving was practical. Astronomers and geodesists routinely needed to minimize a function of several variables when the equations could not be solved analytically. Cauchy's procedure: compute the derivative of the function in each direction at the current point, take a small step in the direction of steepest decrease, then repeat. Follow the slope downhill. Keep going until the slope flattens. He proved it would converge under reasonable conditions and demonstrated it on a small numerical example.

passages.chapter-10-p-3129a58fa3: For roughly the next century, the method sat in textbooks as a numerical curiosity, useful for specific calculations and otherwise unremarkable.
